title: Symbols, Rituals and Sacred Space
bigQuestion: What do rituals, journeys and buildings show about what a tradition holds most important?

story.title: Four Buildings on One Bus Route
story.kicker: A class rides one Chicago bus and learns to read four houses of worship from the outside in.
paragraphs: Mr. Kim's class climbed onto a city bus with notebooks and pencils. Their task was simple to say and hard to do. They would look at four houses of worship along the route, from the outside only. They would write what they saw, and guess what each shape might mean. Then they would check.

The first was a stone church with a tall tower and a cross on top. Seen from above, its floor plan made a cross too. Two blocks later came a mosque with a dome and a slim tower called a minaret. Leila, whose family prays there, said the prayer hall faces Mecca. "Even in Chicago," she said, "everyone faces the same direction."

Next was a synagogue with Hebrew letters over the door and a carved scroll-shaped symbol. Then the bus passed a gurdwara flying a tall orange flag. Arjun pointed. "There is a free meal inside every day," he said. "Anyone can eat." The class wrote down the flag and the open doors.

Back at school, Mr. Kim asked what they had learned. Sofia raised her hand. "A building is like a book," she said. "The shape tells you what the people inside care about." Mr. Kim wrote her words on the board. Then he added one more line: "And the best way to check is to ask them."
story.think: What can you learn about a tradition from the outside of its building? What can you learn only by asking the people inside?

lessons.title: What Makes a Ritual
lessons.mainIdea: A ritual is an action done the same way on purpose, and adherents say it connects them to something they hold sacred.
reading: At a Jewish Friday night dinner, a family lights two candles and says a blessing over bread and wine. They do it the same way every week. An action repeated on purpose, in a set pattern, is called a *ritual*. Rituals can be large, like a festival, or small, like a bow before a meal.

Rituals often use *symbols*. A symbol is an object or action that stands for something bigger. The candles can stand for the rest and holiness of the Sabbath. In many Christian churches, water in baptism stands for washing and new life. A symbol says a lot without many words.

Scholars notice that rituals do several jobs. They mark time. They bind a group together. They pass beliefs from old to young without a lecture. Adherents usually describe rituals in their own terms, as ways of honoring God or following a teacher's path.

words.d: an action done the same way on purpose, often with a religious meaning
an object, picture or action that stands for a bigger idea

look.title: Read the Ritual
look.text: Before eating, a Buddhist monk places his palms together and pauses. A Muslim family says "Bismillah," in the name of God. A Christian family bows heads for a short prayer.
look.prompt: What do these three rituals share? What makes each one belong to its own tradition?

check.q: Which best defines a ritual?
choices: Any action done once by accident
An action done the same way on purpose
check.why: A ritual is a repeated, purposeful pattern of action.

check.q: In many Christian churches, what does baptism water stand for?
check.why: Baptism water is a symbol of washing and new life in Christian teaching.

check.q: What is one job scholars say rituals do?
check.why: Scholars observe that rituals mark time and bind communities together.

lessons.title: Birth and Coming of Age
lessons.mainIdea: Many traditions mark birth and growing up with rites of passage that welcome a person into the community.
reading: A *rite of passage* marks a move from one stage of life to the next. Birth is often the first. In many Muslim families, a parent whispers the call to prayer into a newborn's ear. Many Christian churches baptize babies. Sikh families often choose a baby's name from a letter found by opening the Guru Granth Sahib.

Coming of age is another step. In Judaism, a boy becomes a *bar mitzvah* at 13, which means son of the commandment. In many communities a girl becomes a bat mitzvah at 12 or 13. Often the young person reads from the Torah before the congregation. In many churches, teens take part in confirmation.

Other traditions mark growing up in their own ways. In some Hindu families, a boy receives a sacred thread in a ceremony called upanayana. In Myanmar, many Buddhist boys spend a short time as novice monks. Sikhs of any age may choose Amrit, a ceremony of commitment to the faith.

words.d: a ceremony that marks a move from one stage of life to the next
son of the commandment; a Jewish boy at 13, when he takes on the commandments
in many Christian churches, a ceremony where a young person affirms the faith

look.title: Common Ages for Coming of Age
look.cite: Common practice; ages vary by community
look.prompt: Which rite has the most fixed age? Why might one tradition vary more than another?

check.q: What does bar mitzvah mean?
check.why: Bar mitzvah means son of the commandment.

check.q: Which is a Sikh way of choosing a baby's name?
choices: Opening the Guru Granth Sahib and using the first letter found
Reading a verse from the Analects
check.why: Many Sikh families name a child from a letter found on a randomly opened page of the Guru Granth Sahib.

check.q: What is a rite of passage?
choices: A journey to a holy city
A ceremony marking a move to a new stage of life
check.why: Rites of passage mark life stages such as birth or coming of age.

lessons.title: Marriage and Death
lessons.mainIdea: Traditions mark marriage and death with rituals that express their teachings about love, family and what comes after life.
reading: At a Sikh wedding, the couple walks four times around the Guru Granth Sahib while hymns are sung. This is the *Anand Karaj*, the ceremony of bliss. At a Hindu wedding, the couple often takes seven steps together around a sacred fire. At many Jewish weddings, the couple stands under a canopy called a chuppah.

Death rituals also differ. Many Hindus cremate the body. Some families carry the ashes to a holy river such as the Ganges. Muslims and Jews usually bury the dead quickly, often within a day. In Islam, the body is placed facing Mecca. Christians often hold a funeral that speaks of hope in the resurrection.

After a Jewish funeral, close family *sit shiva*, seven days of mourning at home. Friends bring food and pray with them. A historian compares these rituals without ranking them. Each shows what a tradition teaches about life, loss and community.

words.d: the Sikh wedding ceremony, in which the couple circles the Guru Granth Sahib four times
in Judaism, seven days of mourning at home after a funeral
burning a body after death, often followed by care for the ashes

look.title: Two Weddings, One Circle
look.text: At a Hindu wedding, a couple circles a sacred fire. At a Sikh wedding, a couple circles the Guru Granth Sahib.
look.prompt: Both walk in a circle. What is at the center of each circle, and what might that show about each tradition?

check.q: At a Sikh wedding, what does the couple walk around?
check.why: In the Anand Karaj, the couple circles the Guru Granth Sahib four times.

check.q: What is sitting shiva?
choices: Seven days of Jewish mourning at home
check.why: Shiva is the seven-day mourning period in Judaism.

check.q: Which tradition commonly practices cremation?
check.why: Many Hindus cremate the dead; Muslims and Jews usually bury quickly.

lessons.title: Mecca, Jerusalem and Rome
lessons.mainIdea: A pilgrimage is a journey to a sacred place, and three cities draw pilgrims from Islam, Judaism and Christianity.
reading: Each year, about two million Muslims travel to Mecca in Saudi Arabia for the *Hajj*. It is one of the Five Pillars of Islam. Muslims who are able, in health and money, are expected to go once in their lives. Pilgrims wear simple white clothing and walk seven times around the *Kaaba*, a cube-shaped building at the center of the Great Mosque.

Jerusalem is sacred to three traditions. Many Jews pray at the Western Wall, a remaining wall from the area of the ancient Temple. Christians visit the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, where tradition places Jesus's burial. Muslims pray at the al-Aqsa Mosque, near the Dome of the Rock. One city holds many memories.

Rome draws Catholic Christians to St. Peter's Basilica in Vatican City. Catholic tradition holds that the apostle Peter was buried there. A *pilgrimage* is more than a trip. Pilgrims describe it as a journey of the heart as well as the feet.

words.d: a journey to a sacred place for religious reasons
the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca, expected once in life of those able
the cube-shaped building in Mecca that Muslims face in prayer

look.title: The Call to Pilgrimage
look.text: The Qur'an tells Abraham to call people to the pilgrimage, and says they will come on foot and on lean camels from every distant road.
look.prompt: How does this verse connect the Hajj to Abraham? Why might that connection matter to pilgrims?

check.q: How many times do Hajj pilgrims walk around the Kaaba?
check.why: Pilgrims circle the Kaaba seven times.

check.q: Which place in Jerusalem is a center of Jewish prayer?
check.why: Many Jews pray at the Western Wall, from the area of the ancient Temple.

check.q: Who is expected to go on the Hajj?
choices: Muslims able in health and money, once in life
Only people who live in Mecca
check.why: The Hajj is a pillar for Muslims who are able to make the journey.

lessons.title: Varanasi, Bodh Gaya and Amritsar
lessons.mainIdea: South Asia holds pilgrimage places sacred to Hindus, Buddhists and Sikhs, each tied to a river, a teacher or a Guru.
reading: At dawn in *Varanasi*, Hindu pilgrims walk down stone steps into the Ganges River. Many Hindus regard the Ganges as sacred and bathe in it to purify themselves. Varanasi is one of the oldest living cities in the world. Many Hindus hope to have their ashes placed in the river there.

In Bodh Gaya, Buddhists from around the world sit beneath a large fig tree. According to Buddhist tradition, the Buddha reached enlightenment under a Bodhi tree on this spot. The present tree is said to grow from a descendant of the first. Monks and visitors meditate, chant and leave flowers.

In Amritsar, Sikhs visit the Harmandir Sahib, often called the Golden Temple. It sits in a pool of water and has four doors, one on each side. Sikhs say the doors show that people from every direction and background are welcome. Its kitchen serves free meals to tens of thousands of visitors a day.

words.d: a Hindu holy city on the Ganges River in northern India
the fig tree under which, Buddhists believe, the Buddha reached enlightenment
the Golden Temple in Amritsar, the most visited Sikh gurdwara

look.title: Match the Pilgrim
look.text: Pilgrim A bathes in a river at dawn. Pilgrim B meditates under a tree. Pilgrim C eats a free meal beside a pool of water.
look.prompt: Which city is each pilgrim in, and which tradition does each place belong to?

check.q: Where do Buddhists believe the Buddha reached enlightenment?
check.why: Buddhist tradition places the enlightenment under the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya.

check.q: Why do Sikhs say the Golden Temple has four doors?
choices: To show that people from every direction are welcome
check.why: Sikhs describe the four doors as a sign of welcome to all.

check.q: Which river do Hindu pilgrims bathe in at Varanasi?
check.why: Varanasi lies on the Ganges, which many Hindus regard as sacred.

lessons.title: Church and Mosque
lessons.mainIdea: A church and a mosque are shaped by how their communities worship, from a cross-shaped floor to a wall that points to Mecca.
reading: Many old churches in Europe and America are built in the shape of a cross when seen from above. The long hall where people sit is the *nave*. At the far end is the altar, where many Christians celebrate communion, a meal of bread and wine that remembers Jesus's last supper. Tall towers and stained glass often draw eyes upward.

A *mosque* is shaped by prayer. Inside, one wall points toward Mecca. In it is a small arched niche called the *mihrab*. Muslims pray in straight rows facing that wall. Many mosques have a minaret, a tower from which the call to prayer is given.

Mosques usually contain no pictures of people. Many Muslims hold that God should not be shown in images. Instead, walls are decorated with geometric patterns and Arabic writing from the Qur'an. A historian can read each building as a statement of how its people worship.

words.d: the long central hall of a church, where the congregation sits
a Muslim house of prayer
the niche in a mosque wall that shows the direction of Mecca

look.title: Floor Plans
look.text: Plan 1: a long hall with an altar at one end, and two short arms that make a cross. Plan 2: a wide hall with rows marked on the carpet, all facing a wall with a small arched niche.
look.prompt: Which plan is a church and which is a mosque? Which clues told you?

check.q: What does the mihrab show?
choices: Where the Torah scroll is kept
The place for the sacred fire
Where the free meal is served
check.why: The mihrab marks the qibla, the direction of Mecca.

check.q: Why do many old churches look like a cross from above?
choices: The cross is the central Christian symbol
It was required by Roman law
To hold four doors for all
check.why: The cross recalls Jesus's crucifixion, central to Christian belief.

check.q: Why do most mosques use patterns and Arabic writing instead of pictures of people?
choices: Paint was not allowed in Arabia
The Qur'an has no written form
Many Muslims hold that God should not be shown in images
Mosques are only used on holidays
check.why: Islamic art commonly avoids images of people in worship spaces and favors calligraphy and geometry.

lessons.title: Synagogue and Gurdwara
lessons.mainIdea: A synagogue centers on the Torah scroll, and a gurdwara centers on the Guru Granth Sahib and a shared kitchen.
reading: In a *synagogue*, the most important object is the Torah scroll. It is kept in a cabinet called the ark, usually on the wall facing Jerusalem. A light often burns above it. During services, the scroll is carried to a raised platform called the bimah and read aloud. The building points the community toward its text.

In a *gurdwara*, which means doorway to the Guru, the Guru Granth Sahib rests on a raised seat under a canopy. Sikhs treat it with the respect given to a living teacher. Everyone covers their head and removes their shoes. People sit on the floor together, which Sikhs say shows that all are equal.

Every gurdwara has a *langar*, a free community kitchen. Volunteers cook and serve a vegetarian meal to anyone who comes. Outside stands the Nishan Sahib, a tall flag with the Sikh emblem. It tells travelers that food and shelter can be found inside.

words.d: a Jewish house of prayer, study and gathering
doorway to the Guru; a Sikh house of worship
the free community kitchen of a gurdwara, open to all

look.title: Center of the Room
look.text: In a synagogue, eyes turn to the ark holding the Torah. In a gurdwara, everyone faces the Guru Granth Sahib on its raised seat.
look.prompt: Both rooms are centered on a book. What does that tell you about each tradition?

check.q: Where is the Torah scroll kept in a synagogue?
check.why: The Torah scroll is kept in the ark, often on the wall toward Jerusalem.

check.q: What is the langar?
choices: The raised platform in a synagogue
A free community kitchen in a gurdwara
check.why: Every gurdwara runs a langar that serves free meals to all.

check.q: Why do Sikhs sit on the floor together in a gurdwara?
choices: It shows that all are equal
There is never room for chairs
It faces the direction of Rome
check.why: Sikhs describe sitting together on the floor as a sign of equality.

lessons.title: Mandir and Stupa
lessons.mainIdea: A Hindu mandir leads worshippers toward a small inner shrine, and a Buddhist stupa is a dome that pilgrims walk around.
reading: A Hindu temple, or *mandir*, is often built as a path inward. Worshippers pass through halls toward a small, dim inner room. It holds the *murti*, a sacred image of a deity. Above it rises a tower. Many Hindus see the temple as a home for the deity and come for darshan, seeing and being seen by the divine.

A *stupa* is a Buddhist monument shaped like a dome. Many hold relics, remains or objects linked to the Buddha or a respected teacher. The Great Stupa at Sanchi in India dates in part to the 200s BCE. Pilgrims walk around a stupa clockwise, often chanting or praying as they go.

The two shapes teach different movements. A mandir draws people inward, toward the image at its heart. A stupa invites people around, in a circle of respect. A historian reads both shapes as clues to what their communities practice.

words.d: a Hindu temple
in Hinduism, a sacred image of a deity, honored in worship
a dome-shaped Buddhist monument, often holding relics, that pilgrims walk around

look.title: Inward or Around?
look.text: Visitor A walks through a series of halls toward a small inner room. Visitor B walks slowly in a circle around a large rounded dome, always keeping it on the right.
look.prompt: Which visitor is at a mandir and which at a stupa? How does each movement fit the building?

check.q: What is a murti?
choices: A sacred image of a deity in Hindu worship
check.why: A murti is honored as a sacred image in a Hindu mandir.

check.q: How do pilgrims move at a stupa?
choices: They read a scroll from a platform
check.why: Circling a stupa clockwise is a common Buddhist practice.

check.q: What often lies inside a stupa?
choices: Relics linked to the Buddha or a respected teacher
check.why: Many stupas were built to hold relics.

lessons.title: A Holy Day Each Week
lessons.mainIdea: Judaism, Christianity and Islam each set apart one day of the week, but they choose different days and keep them differently.
reading: The *Sabbath*, or Shabbat, is the Jewish day of rest. It begins at sunset on Friday and ends after dark on Saturday. Many Jews do not work, and families share meals, pray and study. The Torah connects the day to God resting after creation.

Most Christians gather on Sunday, the day they believe Jesus rose from the dead. Many attend worship and rest from work. Muslims gather on Friday for *Jumu'ah*, the midday congregational prayer at a mosque. Many Muslims work on Friday, but they leave time for the prayer and sermon.

So three related traditions set apart three different days. Each one ties its day to a teaching or a story. A calendar, then, is more than a list of dates. It shows what a community remembers together.

words.d: the Jewish day of rest, from Friday sunset to Saturday night
the Friday midday congregational prayer in Islam

look.title: Rest on the Seventh Day
look.text: And on the seventh day God finished His work which He had made; and He rested on the seventh day from all His work which He had made.
look.cite: Genesis 2:2, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society (1917)
look.prompt: How does this verse help explain why the Sabbath is on the seventh day?

check.q: When does the Jewish Sabbath begin?
check.why: Shabbat runs from Friday sunset to Saturday night.

check.q: Why do most Christians gather on Sunday?
choices: The Torah names Sunday as the Sabbath
They believe Jesus rose from the dead on that day
It is the day of Jumu'ah
check.why: Christians connect Sunday worship to the resurrection.

check.q: What is Jumu'ah?
choices: The Friday midday congregational prayer in Islam
check.why: Jumu'ah is the Friday prayer at the mosque.

lessons.title: Fasts and Feasts
lessons.mainIdea: Many traditions follow a time of fasting with a time of feasting, and both teach through the body what a tradition values.
reading: During *Ramadan*, the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, many Muslims fast from dawn to sunset. They take no food or drink during daylight. The Qur'an names Ramadan as the month it was first revealed. At the end comes Eid al-Fitr, a feast of prayer, food and gifts.

On *Yom Kippur*, the Day of Atonement, many Jews fast for about 25 hours and pray for forgiveness. Many Christians keep Lent, forty days before Easter, by giving something up. A *fast* means going without food or other things for a religious reason. Adherents describe fasts as a time to focus on God and on others.

Feasts bring people together. Hindus, Sikhs and Jains celebrate Diwali with lamps and sweets. Jewish families retell the Exodus at the Passover meal, called the seder. Sikhs mark Vaisakhi in spring. Because the Islamic calendar follows the moon, Ramadan moves about eleven days earlier each year.

words.d: the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, when many Muslims fast from dawn to sunset
the Jewish Day of Atonement, a day of fasting and prayer for forgiveness
going without food or other things for a religious reason

look.title: How Long the Fast Lasts
look.cite: Common practice; details vary by community
look.prompt: Which fast is longest? How is a daytime Ramadan fast different from Yom Kippur's full-day fast?

check.q: During Ramadan, when do many Muslims fast?
check.why: The Ramadan fast runs through the daylight hours.

check.q: Which holiday is the Jewish Day of Atonement?
check.why: Yom Kippur is a day of fasting and prayer for forgiveness.

check.q: Why does Ramadan move about eleven days earlier each year?
choices: The Islamic calendar follows the moon
check.why: A lunar year is about eleven days shorter than a solar year.

review.q: Which is a rite of passage?
review.why: A bar mitzvah marks coming of age, a move to a new life stage.

review.q: Which place is sacred to Jews, Christians and Muslims?
review.why: Jerusalem holds sacred sites of all three traditions.

review.q: Which building feature matches its tradition?
review.why: The langar is the free kitchen of a gurdwara.

review.q: Where do Hindu pilgrims bathe in a sacred river?
Which day do Muslims gather for congregational prayer?
review.why: Jumu'ah is the Friday midday prayer.

choices: A journey to a sacred place
review.why: A pilgrimage is a religious journey to a sacred place.
Eid al-Fitr celebrates the end of the Ramadan fast.

review.q: A Sikh couple walks four times around a sacred book. What is this?
review.why: The Anand Karaj is the Sikh wedding ceremony.
